concepts.statement: How the field nests: machine learning is a subset of AI, deep learning a subset of ML built on neural networks; generative AI and agentic AI are newer branches, and a language model earns 'large' through parameter and training-data scale

Telling the working parts apart: the algorithm is the procedure that learns, the model is the artifact it produces; training is the phase that learns from data, inferencing is the phase that predicts on new input

Matching a problem to a learning approach using two signals: whether the data carries labels (supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement) and what shape the output takes — a number for regression, a class for classification, groups for clustering

Choosing how a model is served: inference mode (batch, real-time, asynchronous, serverless) follows the workload's latency and volume shape, and managed API versus self-hosted decides who carries the operational responsibility

Recognizing a dataset's type from its description — tabular, time-series, image, or text — and separately whether it is structured or unstructured, since structure and modality are different properties

Judging whether AI is the right tool at all: it earns its cost where it assists human decisions, scales a solution, or automates work — and is the wrong choice when a deterministic answer is required or the cost-benefit analysis fails
Naming the AI application category behind a described product capability — computer vision, NLP, speech recognition, recommendation, fraud detection, forecasting — before any service is chosen
Selecting the AWS AI service that performs the required job — task-level managed services against stack-level platforms — with each candidate separated from near neighbors that perform adjacent jobs
Preferring traditional ML or a small model over a foundation model when regulation, explainability requirements, or operational constraints such as edge or offline deployment dominate the decision

Placing work at the right stage of the AI/ML pipeline — EDA, data pre-processing, feature engineering, training, hyperparameter tuning, evaluation, deployment, monitoring — and telling adjacent stages apart
Where a model comes from: reusing an open source pre-trained model saves the time, data, and compute of training a custom model, at the price of less task fit and less control
MLOps as a discipline of repeatability — experimentation, repeatable processes, scalable systems, managed technical debt, production readiness — rather than a particular toolchain
Why a deployed model degrades as production data drifts from what it was trained on, and why the response is model monitoring feeding scheduled or triggered re-training

Evaluating a model on both halves: pick the model-performance metric (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) that fits the task and its error costs, and pair it with the business metrics (ROI, cost per user, customer feedback) that measure value
A token is the unit of text a language model reads and generates; context windows and usage are counted in tokens, not words or characters
Retrieval foundations: an embedding encodes meaning as a vector so similarity becomes geometric distance, and chunking splits documents into retrievable pieces whose size shapes what can be found
Prompt engineering shapes model behavior through the input alone — no weights change — which is what separates it from every form of tuning

What makes a model a foundation model — broad pre-training adaptable to many tasks, transformer-based for language — and choosing a family by modality: multi-modal models span input types, diffusion models generate images

Recognizing a GenAI use case by the new artifact it produces — summaries, code, conversation, images — and the capabilities behind the fit: adaptability, responsiveness, and content generation where rule systems would need rewriting
The FM lifecycle in order — data selection, model selection, pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment, feedback — and which activities belong to which stage

GenAI economics as a design input: token-based pricing makes prompt and output length a cost decision, and provisioned throughput versus on-demand inference is the lever when load, not model quality, is the problem
Context engineering assembles and prioritizes what goes into a model call — retrieved content, history, instructions — distinct from wording a prompt and from changing weights by fine-tuning
What an agent adds beyond a single FM call: tool usage to act, memory management to persist state, and workflow orchestration to sequence multi-step work
Structuring more than one agent: multi-agent system patterns divide work among specialized agents, and communication patterns govern how they coordinate and hand off
Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the open protocol that connects agents and assistants to external tools and data sources through a standard interface
Hallucination: fluent, confident output that is wrong — a first-class GenAI failure mode to plan controls around, not an occasional bug
Nondeterminism: the same prompt need not return the same answer, which breaks workflows that assume repeatability and has to be designed for rather than discovered in production
Selecting a foundation model against competing constraints — capability, cost, latency, compliance, model complexity — where no single score decides and the binding constraint does

Choosing the AWS GenAI building block for the job: Amazon Bedrock as the managed FM platform, SageMaker AI and JumpStart for custom work, Amazon Q as the packaged assistant, Strands Agents and Bedrock AgentCore for agents

Why a managed GenAI service beats self-assembly for a team without ML infrastructure: lower barrier to entry and speed to market, plus platform-inherited security, compliance, and safety a self-built stack would have to earn
Selecting an FM by the requirement that dominates the workload — cost, modality, latency, multi-lingual support, model size and complexity, customization options, input/output length
Prompt caching reuses a repeated prompt prefix across calls, cutting cost and latency exactly when many requests share the same leading context

Which inference parameter moves which property of the output: temperature widens or narrows sampling randomness, candidate-set limits trim what can be sampled, and length settings cap the response — none of them changes what the model knows

Retrieval Augmented Generation grounds answers in documents retrieved at question time — the fix for private or fast-changing knowledge, because the weights never contained it and retraining cannot keep up
Where embeddings are stored and searched on AWS — Amazon OpenSearch Service, Aurora, Neptune, RDS for PostgreSQL — a vector-store decision separate from choosing the embedding model
Ranking customization approaches by cost and effort: in-context learning is cheapest, then RAG, then fine-tuning, then pre-training — with model distillation as the route to a smaller, cheaper model
What an AI agent is for in business terms: completing a multi-step task by orchestrating tool and API calls — a coordinator of actions, not a better model
The anatomy of a working prompt — context, instruction, and negative prompts — and the craft that improves it: specificity and concision, refined through experimentation and discovery

Naming the prompting technique from a described setup: zero-shot, single-shot, or few-shot by the number of in-prompt examples; chain-of-thought when reasoning is asked to be shown; prompt templates for reuse

Telling adversarial prompt risks apart by the attacker's objective: exposure leaks data, poisoning corrupts training or retrieval content, hijacking repurposes the system, jailbreaking defeats its safety policy
Treating prompts as versioned, managed artifacts — tracked, compared, and rolled back like code — with Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management as the AWS home for it

The four ways a model's weights change, told apart by purpose: pre-training builds general capability, fine-tuning adapts to a task, continuous pre-training extends domain knowledge, distillation compresses into a smaller model

Fine-tuning variants named by objective: instruction tuning teaches a model to follow directions, domain adaptation specializes it to a field's language, transfer learning reuses learned capability on a new task
What fine-tuning data must look like before quality can follow: curated, governed, sufficiently sized, labeled, and representative of the traffic the model will actually see
Reinforcement learning from human feedback aligns model behavior with human preference rankings, used where no labeled right answer exists to train against

Choosing an FM evaluation approach to fit the quality criterion: human-in-the-loop when the bar is subjective, benchmark datasets for comparability, LLM-as-a-judge for scale — with Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation as tooling

Matching a generation metric to what it actually measures: ROUGE for summarization overlap, BLEU for translation quality, BERTScore for semantic similarity — none of them certifies factual correctness
Evaluating the application rather than the model: a RAG pipeline, agent, or workflow is judged end-to-end, because component quality does not compose into system quality

Measuring whether the AI application serves the business: task completion rate, user satisfaction, cost per interaction, conversion — the alignment metrics that decide value where benchmark scores cannot
The named dimensions of responsible AI — bias, fairness, inclusivity, robustness, safety, veracity — and the dataset characteristics that deliver them: diverse, curated, balanced data

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as the control that enforces content and topic policy on model interactions — constraining behavior at the boundary of the prompt and the output rather than by retraining the model
Model choice as an environmental decision: larger models cost more energy to train and to run, so sustainability is a legitimate selection criterion rather than an afterthought
The legal and business exposure GenAI creates: intellectual property infringement claims from generated output, biased outputs, end user risk, and the loss of customer trust that follows

Reading a model's fit from its scores: strong training but weak validation or production performance means overfitting, weak on both means underfitting — and either failure can fall unevenly across demographic groups
How bias is actually found in practice: subgroup analysis of per-group accuracy, analysis of label quality, and human audits — with Amazon A2I bringing human review into the loop
Transparent and explainable are different properties: transparency exposes what the system is and how it was built; explainability accounts for why a particular output happened

The artifacts and mechanisms that carry explainability to people: SageMaker Model Cards documenting purpose and limitations, SageMaker Clarify surfacing bias and attributions, open source and licensing disclosure, and human-centered design with user feedback loops
The safety-transparency trade-off: the models that perform best are often the hardest to interpret, so a regulated or high-stakes decision can force a more interpretable, lower-performing choice

Access control as the first AI security control: least-privilege IAM roles, policies, and permissions on data, models, and endpoints — extended to agents specifically through Bedrock AgentCore Identity and Policy
Protecting data and model artifacts in place and in motion: encryption at rest and in transit with managed keys, and AWS PrivateLink to keep model traffic off the public internet
vocabulary: encryption at rest and in transit

concepts.statement: Secure data engineering before the model sees anything: discover sensitive data with Amazon Macie, apply privacy-enhancing technologies and data access control, and preserve data quality and integrity
Who is responsible for what: the AWS shared responsibility model, and the Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix that adjusts the split by how much of the GenAI stack you own
Stopping bad output before the user sees it: data leakage prevention, output filtering and validation, toxicity controls, and hallucination detection through grounding and confidence scoring
Prompt injection: untrusted text carrying instructions the model obeys — the GenAI-native attack, countered at the input boundary rather than by retraining
Knowing where an answer came from and proving it later: source citation and data lineage on the way in, audit trails and logging of AI interactions on the way out
vocabulary: audit trail and logging requirements for AI interactions

concepts.statement: Which AWS service answers which governance and security-posture question: Config for resource compliance, Inspector for vulnerabilities, Artifact for compliance reports, CloudTrail for API history, Trusted Advisor for best-practice checks
Data governance as an operated lifecycle: residency, retention, logging, and monitoring obligations, kept working through policies, review cadence, and team training
